meaning_fix: full (m.) / filled up; 'fed up' is normally said zahqaan or tafshaan
reasoning: Standard Palestinian malyaan, 'full'. It can be used figuratively (full of anger), but plain 'fed up' is not its main sense.

The word is pronounced with a doubled b (kubbaaye), though the spelling shows one ب. Taa marbuta after ي is e. The vowel of the first syllable varies between speakers (kubbaaye/kibbaaye); kaase is a synonym.
MSA-origin academic word that Palestinians use normally. ظ is emphatic TH, the shadda doubles y, and taa marbuta after y is e.

meaning_fix: the weather is icy / snowy (a state); 'it's snowing' is said 3am bitthallij
reasoning: The participle مثلجة with ث is literary. Native Palestinian 'snow' is talj, so I gave the colloquial-style form, but I am not sure a Ramallah speaker would say it at all. For 'it's snowing' a verb with 3am is more natural.
MSA-origin word in normal Palestinian use. The medial hamza is a glottal stop. Some speakers say tawaam, but taw'am is standard.
il- assimilates to ت, mish negates the participle, and shaghghaale is feminine with doubled gh. The spelling suggests tadfi'a, but tadfiye is also heard. Taa marbuta after the hamza is a.
The word is in everyday use for property and real estate (plural 3a'aaraat). I took ق as a glottal stop, though a formal register may keep q. 'Real estate / property' is accurate.

meaning_fix: the press / journalism (media in general is إعلام)
reasoning: ص is emphatic S and ح is 7. Taa marbuta after ف is e. Si7aafe means journalism or the press, not media generally.
The Levantine month name for September is used in Palestine. I have uu in the last syllable, like tammuuz; the initial hamza is just a vowel seat.
MSA-origin political title that Palestinians use as is. Medial and final hamza are both glottal stops; the long vowel in ra'iis is ii.
Palestinians say 7eefa with long ee, not MSA 7ayfaa. ح is 7.
After numbers 3–10 Palestinians say talaaf, with a linking t, instead of aalaaf. The number form 3ashar is used before it; 3ashart alaaf is a variant.
Common English loan for a mobile phone, with long oo and aa. The final vowel is reduced in fast speech.
The plural imperative of Form VIII loses its middle i (ittaSil → ittaSlu). ص is emphatic. 3a + il- joins as 3al-, and the hamza of is3aaf is written after the article.
Doubled w at the end, as in Palestinian 3aduww. The word is MSA in origin but used in ordinary speech.
MSA-origin word that keeps th. ق is a glottal stop in everyday use, and taa marbuta after ق is a. Some speakers may say ti'a or si'a.
The dual of miyye (100) is miiteen, with long ii in the first syllable and ee in the dual ending.
ba- (I) + b3at + -lak (to you, m.), with the b- prefix giving bab3atlak. masij is the usual loan from English 'message'; its exact vowels vary between speakers.
This is a literary political term, so I kept q. The verb in'alab is glottal in everyday use, and some speakers say in'ilaab. The initial hamza is a vowel seat, so it is not written.
Palestinian silaa7 with short i, ح as 7 and long aa. It means weapon or arms, and includes guns.
Formal 'now', deliberately labelled MSA. A Ramallah speaker says halla'. Romanized without case endings and with the Palestinian article il-.
Imperative of qaSS is 'uSS, with ق as a glottal stop and doubled emphatic S. li means 'for me'. shwayy is 'a bit'. ج is a moon letter, so il-jawaanib.
English loan 'user' used in Palestinian for a username or account name. Long uu in the first syllable; some speakers say yoozar or yoozer.
Levantine yaa reet, with long ee from MSA layta. It is common in Palestinian speech.
ض is emphatic D. The colloquial word for 'clean' is naDiif (MSA naDHiif), and some speakers reduce it to nDiif.
